cards.front: Water's oxygen end is slightly {{c1::negative}} and its hydrogen ends are slightly positive, so neighboring water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.
cards.back: That uneven spread of charge is what makes water polar.
cards.quote: Water's oxygen end is slightly negative and its hydrogen ends are slightly positive, so neighboring water molecules attract each other through hydrogen bonds.
cards.section: Explain: a molecule with charged ends

cards.front: What holds the two hydrogen atoms to the oxygen atom inside one water molecule?
cards.back: Covalent bonds, in which the atoms share electrons.
cards.quote: A water molecule has covalent bonds (shared electrons) inside it, partial charges that make it polar, and hydrogen bonds
cards.section: Explain: a molecule with charged ends

cards.front: What is a hydrogen bond between two water molecules?
cards.back: A weak pull between the slightly positive hydrogen of one water molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of a neighbor.
cards.why: It links separate molecules, unlike the covalent bonds inside one molecule.
cards.quote: hydrogen bonds, the weak pulls between the slightly positive hydrogen of one molecule and the slightly negative oxygen of a neighbor
cards.section: Explain: a molecule with charged ends

cards.front: A {{c1::solvent}} is a liquid that dissolves other substances.
cards.quote: A solvent is a liquid that dissolves other substances.

cards.front: When table salt dissolves in water, what holds the sodium and chloride ions to the water molecules?
cards.back: The pull of opposite charges: water's slightly negative oxygen ends face the positive sodium ions, and its slightly positive hydrogen ends face the negative chloride ions. It is not hydrogen bonding.
cards.quote: The first film's salt ions, charged particles, are held by the pull of opposite charges, not by hydrogen bonds.

cards.front: Sugar has no ions. Why does it still dissolve in water?
cards.back: Sugar molecules carry slightly charged hydrogens and oxygens, like water's, so water forms hydrogen bonds with sugar and pulls the molecules apart.
cards.quote: Sugar has no ions, but its molecules carry slightly charged hydrogens and oxygens like water's, so water hydrogen-bonds to sugar and dissolves it.

cards.front: Why does cooking oil stay in its own layer instead of dissolving in water?
cards.back: Oil molecules are mostly nonpolar, sharing their electrons about evenly. Water hydrogen-bonds with itself but hardly at all with oil, so the water molecules stay together and leave the oil out.
cards.quote: The film's oil is nonpolar: its molecules share their electrons about evenly.

cards.front: A classmate says water is the universal solvent, so it will dissolve candle wax. Candle wax is made of mostly nonpolar molecules. Predict what happens when the wax sits in water, and explain.
cards.back: The wax does not dissolve. Water attracts charged and polar particles, but nonpolar molecules have no charged ends for water to pull on, so water keeps bonding with itself instead.
cards.why: Rule: water dissolves charged and polar substances; it does not dissolve everything.
cards.quote: Water is sometimes called the universal solvent, but it does not dissolve everything.

cards.front: {{c1::Cohesion}} is the attraction of water molecules to each other; at the surface it gives surface tension, the surface's resistance to being stretched.
cards.quote: Cohesion is the attraction of water molecules to each other; at the surface it gives surface tension, the surface's resistance to being stretched.

cards.front: {{c1::Adhesion}} is the attraction of water to a different substance.
cards.back: It is strong on polar surfaces such as cellulose in paper and plant cell walls.
cards.quote: Adhesion is the attraction of water to a different substance.

cards.front: A water strider stands on a pond without sinking. Explain how cohesion and the strider's leg hairs both help.
cards.back: Cohesion at the surface gives surface tension, so the surface resists being stretched. The leg hairs are water-repellent, so adhesion to them is weak and water beads up instead of wetting the legs.
cards.quote: weak on water-repellent ones such as the strider's leg hairs, where water beads up.

cards.front: When adhesion and cohesion together pull water up a narrow space or a fiber, that is {{c1::capillary action}}.
cards.back: Example: water climbing up a paper towel.
cards.quote: When adhesion and cohesion together pull water up a narrow space or a fiber, that is capillary action.

cards.front: In a tall tree, what supplies most of the lift that moves water up from the roots, and what do cohesion and adhesion do?
cards.back: Water evaporating at the leaves (transpiration) pulls the column up. Cohesion keeps the water column in the xylem whole, and adhesion to the tube walls helps hold it in place.
cards.quote: In a tall tree, most of the lift comes from water evaporating at the leaves (transpiration), which pulls the column up

cards.front: One paper strip is plain; an identical strip is coated with a water-repellent wax. Both are dipped in water. Predict which strip water climbs higher, and why.
cards.back: Water should climb higher on the plain strip. Plain paper is polar cellulose, so adhesion is strong; on the waxed strip adhesion is weak, so water should climb less. This is a prediction to test.
cards.why: Rule: capillary action needs adhesion and cohesion together.
cards.quote: It is strong on polar surfaces such as cellulose, in plant cell walls and paper

cards.front: A pond freezes over in winter. Predict whether the ice sinks or floats, and say why it matters to fish.
cards.back: The ice floats. Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules of ice in an open pattern, so the same mass takes up more space and ice is less dense than liquid water. A deep enough pond keeps liquid water underneath, where fish survive.
cards.quote: The same mass takes up more space, so ice is less dense, with less mass in each cubic centimetre, than liquid water.

cards.front: What does the temperature of a substance measure?
cards.back: The average energy of motion of the substance's particles.
cards.quote: temperature (the average energy of motion of a substance's particles)
cards.section: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed

cards.front: What is specific heat, and about what is it for liquid water and for dry sand?
cards.back: The energy to warm one gram by 1 °C. About 4.18 joules per gram per degree for liquid water, and about 0.8 for dry sand.
cards.quote: specific heat (the energy to warm one gram by 1 °C: about 4.18 joules per gram per degree for liquid water
cards.section: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed

cards.front: How is heat capacity different from specific heat?
cards.back: Specific heat is the energy to warm one gram by 1 °C. Heat capacity is the energy to warm a whole object by 1 °C; for one substance, it is mass times specific heat.
cards.quote: heat capacity (the energy to warm a whole object by 1 °C; for one substance, mass times specific heat)
cards.section: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed

cards.front: Why does each gram of liquid water need so much energy to warm up?
cards.back: Much of the added energy goes into rearranging the web of hydrogen bonds between water molecules, not only into making the molecules move faster.
cards.quote: in water, rearranging the web of hydrogen bonds is a big part of the high specific heat.

cards.front: 250 grams of liquid water take in 2092 joules. Using a specific heat of 4.184 J per gram per °C, by how much does the water's temperature rise?
cards.back: Temperature change = heat ÷ (mass × specific heat) = 2092 ÷ (250 × 4.184) = 2.0 °C.
cards.quote: Temperature change = heat ÷ (mass × specific heat).
cards.section: The heat calculation, step by step

cards.front: In the water-and-sand heater simulation, a beaker of dry sand warms by 15 °C. An equal mass of water gets the same energy. About how much does the water warm? (Water about 4.18, dry sand about 0.8 J per gram per °C.)
cards.back: Same energy and mass, so the rise scales as 1 ÷ specific heat: 15 × 0.8 ÷ 4.18 ≈ 2.9 °C, about 3 °C, roughly one fifth of the sand's rise.
cards.quote: equal energy warms water about one fifth as much as an equal mass of dry sand, as in your simulation
cards.section: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed

cards.front: Two ponds of the same area get the same sunshine all day. One is 0.5 m deep, the other 5 m deep, and each mixes its warmth through its whole depth. Which warms more, and about how many times more?
cards.back: The shallow pond, about ten times as much: the same energy goes into a tenth of the mass, as long as neither pond loses much heat to the ground or air.
cards.why: Rule: the same energy in more grams gives a proportionally smaller rise.
cards.quote: Grow the mass: the same energy in more grams gives a proportionally smaller rise.
cards.section: Explain: why the Bay barely warmed

cards.front: Besides the specific heat of each gram, what makes a whole lake or bay warm even more slowly?
cards.back: Its huge mass, its mixing, and evaporation. Specific heat is a necessary part of the story, not the whole of it.
cards.quote: how slowly a whole lake or bay warms also depends on its mass, mixing and evaporation.

cards.front: At the Stingray Point buoy in the Chesapeake Bay on July 9, 2025, eight readings every third hour gave air temperatures from 23.0 °C to 30.1 °C and water temperatures from 28.6 °C to 29.8 °C. Find each range and how many times larger the air's range is.
cards.back: Air: 30.1 − 23.0 = 7.1 °C. Water: 29.8 − 28.6 = 1.2 °C. Ratio: 7.1 ÷ 1.2 ≈ 5.9, so the air's range is about six times the water's.
cards.quote: Find the range of the air temperatures in the table (highest minus lowest).
cards.section: Elaborate: air and water at a Bay buoy

cards.front: Just after 2 a.m. at a Chesapeake Bay buoy, a gust of cooler wind dropped the air temperature by 3 to 5 °C within about an hour. Predict what the water just below the surface did, and why.
cards.back: The water barely changed, consistent with water's high specific heat (each gram needs a lot of energy to change temperature). The buoy data cannot separate specific heat from the Bay's mass, mixing and evaporation.
cards.quote: the water barely changed through both gusts.
cards.section: Elaborate: air and water at a Bay buoy

cards.front: Equal masses of water and dry sand have been heated, and the heater is turned off. If both lose energy at the same rate, which cools faster, and why? What changes the answer outdoors?
cards.back: The sand cools faster: it needs less energy loss per degree, because its specific heat is lower. Outdoors, wind, surface area and evaporation set the rates of loss, so the comparison can change.
cards.quote: The film's cooling answer assumes both lose energy at the same rate; outdoors, wind, surface area and evaporation set those rates.

cards.front: At the Chesapeake Bay buoy, the air's temperature range was about 6 times the water's, close to the ratio of water's specific heat to dry sand's (about 5). Does that mean the air over the Bay behaves like the sand in the simulation?
cards.back: No. Land, wind and gusts helped set the air's swing, and the water's steadiness also depends on the Bay's mass, mixing and evaporation. The two ratios measure different things, so their closeness is a coincidence.
cards.quote: The ratios measure different things, so their closeness is a coincidence.
cards.section: Elaborate: air and water at a Bay buoy

cards.front: Plan a fair test of whether the width of a paper strip changes how high water climbs it. Name the independent and dependent variables, three constants, and how you would handle trials.
cards.back: Independent: strip width (for example 5, 10 and 20 mm). Dependent: height reached after 10 minutes, in mm from the water line. Constants: paper from one sheet, strip length, dipping depth, the water and its temperature. At least five strips per width; compare means.
cards.quote: Plan a fair test you could do with paper, a ruler, a tray of water and a timer.

cards.front: Your body is roughly half water by weight. A runner's working muscles make heat. Explain two ways body water limits swings in body temperature.
cards.back: Blood, mostly water, carries heat from warm muscles to cooler parts of the body. The water in tissues needs a lot of energy per degree, so it slows temperature changes, along with sweating and other controls.
cards.quote: Blood, which is mostly water, carries heat from warm working muscles to cooler parts of the body

cards.front: Name the attraction at work in each case: a water strider on a pond, water climbing a paper towel, salt dissolving, and the Chesapeake Bay warming slowly.
cards.back: Strider: water to water (cohesion, surface tension). Towel: water to a polar surface (adhesion), with cohesion. Salt: water to ions (opposite charges). Bay: water to water, hydrogen bonds raising specific heat, and the Bay's mass, mixing and evaporation help too.
cards.quote: which attraction (water to water, to a polar surface, or to an ion) is at work in the strider, the towel, the salt and the Bay?
